summary: Find the sum of three numbers in the array that is closest to the target.
mainInsight: Sort, fix one number, then use two pointers on the rest: the pair sum is monotone in each pointer, so move l when the total is below the target and r when above, tracking the closest total seen.

approaches.name: Sort + fix one + two pointers
approaches.summary: For each i sweep l/r over the suffix, updating the closest sum.

personalSolution.notes: Optimal. You could skip duplicate i values as a micro-optimisation.

promptVariants: Which approach gives O(n^2) for 3Sum Closest?
options: Sort the array, then two pointers for each fixed element
Hash set lookup of the needed complement for every pair of numbers
Variable-size sliding window over the sorted array of values
Breadth-first search over the states of partial sums
cards.answer: Sort the array, then two pointers for each fixed element
cards.explanation: Same skeleton as 3Sum, but compare |target - total| instead of testing equality.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Hash set lookup of the needed complement: A set finds exact matches; closeness needs ordering.

promptVariants: Why can't a hash set be used here but two pointers can?
What does sorting give you for 'closest' queries?
cards.answer: Closest requires order: with sorted numbers the pair sum increases when l moves right and decreases when r moves left, steering the sum toward the target. A hash set only answers exact equality.
keyPoints: Monotone sum in l and r
cards.explanation: Same reason Two Sum II uses two pointers.
n two-pointer sweeps of O(n) each; the sort is O(n log n).

promptVariants: What is the extra space, and what can inflate it?
What auxiliary memory does 3Sum Closest need, and what hidden cost does sorting add?
cards.answer: O(1) besides the sort (Python's sort can use O(n)). No hash structures are needed.

promptVariants: Why is the closest-sum update placed after the pointer move yet still uses `total`?
Why can the loop return immediately when total == target?
cards.answer: `total` was computed before the pointer moved and is the sum actually evaluated, so comparing it against best is correct regardless of where the update sits. An exact hit has distance 0, which nothing can beat, so returning early is safe.
cards.explanation: Updating before moving the pointers reads more naturally.

promptVariants: Why initialise best = float('inf') instead of a number from the array?
What happens with exactly three elements?
options: Any real sum is closer than infinity, so the first sum replaces it
Infinity is required so that the array can be sorted in place first
It avoids an integer overflow when adding three large values
It makes the loop run exactly once for every starting index
cards.answer: Any real sum is closer than infinity, so the first sum replaces it
cards.explanation: abs(target - inf) is infinite, so the first evaluated total always becomes best. (With 3 elements the only triple is evaluated and returned.)
